17// Encoder turns I420 frames into H.264 access units in Annex-B form.
18type Encoder interface {
19 // Encode compresses one frame taken at ts since the stream started. It
20 // may return no data when the rate controller skips the frame.
21 Encode(img *yuv.I420, ts time.Duration, keyframe bool) ([]byte, error)
22 SetBitrate(bps int) error
23 Close() error
24}
25
26// NewEncoderFunc builds an encoder for one frame size. The session recreates
27// the encoder whenever the display is resized.
28type NewEncoderFunc func(width, height, fps, bitrate int) (Encoder, error)
29
30// minKeyframeGap bounds how often loss reports can force an IDR frame: each
31// one is large, and a burst of them would deepen the congestion that caused
32// the loss.
33const minKeyframeGap = 300 * time.Millisecond
34
35// stream captures, encodes and sends frames at up to fps while a peer is
36// attached. An idle screen costs one cheap DAMAGE check per tick.
37type stream struct {
38 desk desktop.Desktop
39 fps int
40 // maxW and maxH cap the encoded size. A spawned display never exceeds
41 // them; an attached one can, and its frames are scaled down to fit.
42 maxW, maxH int
43 newEncoder NewEncoderFunc
44 log *slog.Logger
45
46 peer atomic.Pointer[peer.Peer]
47 keyframe atomic.Bool
48 bitrate atomic.Int64
49 // scale is how frames are shrunk on their way out, nil while they go
50 // out at desktop size.
51 scale atomic.Pointer[scale]
52}
53
54// scale is a desktop size and the smaller one its frames are encoded at.
55type scale struct{ deskW, deskH, w, h int }
56
57// toDesktop maps the position in a pointer event, which the page reports in
58// video pixels, to the desktop pixel at the centre of that video pixel.
59func (s *stream) toDesktop(m protocol.Control) protocol.Control {
60 sc := s.scale.Load()
61 if sc == nil || (m.T != protocol.ControlMove && m.T != protocol.ControlButton) {
62 return m
63 }
64 m.X = min((2*m.X+1)*sc.deskW/(2*sc.w), sc.deskW-1)
65 m.Y = min((2*m.Y+1)*sc.deskH/(2*sc.h), sc.deskH-1)
66 return m
67}
68
69func newStream(desk desktop.Desktop, fps, maxW, maxH int, newEncoder NewEncoderFunc, log *slog.Logger) *stream {
70 s := &stream{desk: desk, fps: fps, maxW: maxW, maxH: maxH, newEncoder: newEncoder, log: log}
71 s.bitrate.Store(startBitrate)
72 return s
73}
74
75func (s *stream) setPeer(p *peer.Peer) {
76 s.peer.Store(p)
77 s.keyframe.Store(true)
78}
79
80func (s *stream) requestKeyframe() { s.keyframe.Store(true) }

12// Retransmission limits. Packets older than nackMaxAge would arrive too late
13// to help a live desktop, and an unbounded responder turns a burst of loss
14// into a retransmission storm: everything lost gets resent, mostly lost
15// again, and congestion control reads the storm as permanent heavy loss.
16const (
17 nackHistory = 512 // packets kept per stream; a power of two
18 nackMaxAge = time.Second
19 nackMaxResends = 2
20 nackBudgetShare = 0.25 // of the congestion controller's target
21 nackBurst = 100 * time.Millisecond
22)
23
24// nackResponderFactory builds the responder for each peer connection.
25// budget reports the current target bitrate in bits per second.
26type nackResponderFactory struct {
27 budget func() int
28}
29
30func (f *nackResponderFactory) NewInterceptor(string) (interceptor.Interceptor, error) {
31 return &nackResponder{budget: f.budget, streams: map[uint32]*sendHistory{}}, nil
32}
33
34// nackResponder answers RTCP NACKs from a short history of sent packets,
35// within a share of the current bitrate.
36type nackResponder struct {
37 interceptor.NoOp
38 budget func() int
39
40 mu sync.Mutex
41 streams map[uint32]*sendHistory
42 tokens float64 // bits
43 refill time.Time
44}
45
46type sentPacket struct {
47 header rtp.Header
48 payload []byte
49 sentAt time.Time
50 resends int
51}
52
53type sendHistory struct {
54 writer interceptor.RTPWriter
55 packets [nackHistory]*sentPacket
56}
57
58func (r *nackResponder) BindLocalStream(info *interceptor.StreamInfo, writer interceptor.RTPWriter) interceptor.RTPWriter {
59 if !wantsNack(info) {
60 return writer
61 }
62 h := &sendHistory{writer: writer}
63 r.mu.Lock()
64 r.streams[info.SSRC] = h
65 r.mu.Unlock()
66 return interceptor.RTPWriterFunc(func(header *rtp.Header, payload []byte, a interceptor.Attributes) (int, error) {
67 p := &sentPacket{header: header.Clone(), payload: append([]byte(nil), payload...), sentAt: time.Now()}
68 r.mu.Lock()
69 h.packets[header.SequenceNumber%nackHistory] = p
70 r.mu.Unlock()
71 return writer.Write(header, payload, a)
72 })
73}
74
75func (r *nackResponder) UnbindLocalStream(info *interceptor.StreamInfo) {
76 r.mu.Lock()
77 delete(r.streams, info.SSRC)
78 r.mu.Unlock()
79}

What the host needs

Linux on x86_64 or arm64, an SSH server you can log in to, and for the headless session: `Xvfb` plus something to run in it, either a desktop (`xfce4-session`) or a window manager (`openbox`, `fluxbox`, `icewm`, `twm`) with a terminal (`xterm`). If anything is missing the CLI says what, with the install line for that distro, for example:

sudo apt install xvfb openbox xterm

Attaching to a running desktop needs none of that, only the desktop, plus GStreamer's tools for a Wayland one.

For sound in a spawned session the host also needs `pulseaudio`. The agent starts a private one with a null sink as its only output and its socket in the agent's run directory, so it touches neither the sound hardware nor a sound server you already run, and it stops with the session. Attached to a running desktop, the agent records that desktop's own sound server instead, PulseAudio or PipeWire alike, since PipeWire speaks the same protocol through `pipewire-pulse`.

No GPU or monitor is needed; the session renders in software, and a light window manager keeps that cheap. Software H.264 at 1080p30 costs one to two cores, which is why small hosts get a lower default size and frame rate.

The agent goes to `~/.cache/robin` (or `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/robin`, or `/tmp/robin-$UID` when the home directory is mounted `noexec`), checked by hash and reused across sessions. It runs as you, starts its own display on a free number, and when the SSH channel closes it kills everything it started and removes its files.

Attaching to a Wayland desktop

`--attach wayland` streams the GNOME or KDE Plasma session you are logged in to on the host instead of starting a new one. It goes through xdg-desktop-portal, the same screen sharing a video call app uses, which means the desktop asks before anyone sees it. `--attach auto` picks it when the session logind reports as active is a Wayland one.

The first time, a dialog comes up on the host's own screen and someone sitting there has to answer it. On GNOME, switch on Allow Remote Interaction before pressing Share, or the session is view only; the CLI says so if that happens, and also says, while it waits, what to approve and for how long (two minutes). KDE Plasma asks once for both the picture and the input, and Approve grants them together. Approval gets the agent a restore token from the portal. The agent keeps it next to itself on the host, in `wayland-restore-token`, readable only by you, and every later session starts with no dialog at all. Delete the file to be asked again. A view-only approval is never remembered, so the next run asks once more.

Ending the session gives the screen back as it was. Stopping the share from the host's own indicator ends the remote session too. Sound comes along as it does on X11, recorded from PipeWire's PulseAudio server, which current GNOME and Plasma desktops run.

The agent reads the screen through GStreamer, so the host needs `gst-launch-1.0` and the PipeWire, base and good plugin sets. A desktop install usually has everything but the tools package; the CLI checks and prints the line for your distribution, for example:

sudo apt install gstreamer1.0-tools gstreamer1.0-pipewire gstreamer1.0-plugins-base gstreamer1.0-plugins-good

Streaming a fully animated 1280x720 screen at 30 fps costs `gst-launch-1.0` about 6% of one core, on top of the encoder. An idle screen costs next to nothing: repeated frames are not encoded.

Hardware encoding

robin gui --max-size 3840x2160 build-box # auto: the GPU, if build-box has one robin gui --encoder vaapi build-box # Intel or AMD through VA-API, or fail robin gui --encoder nvenc gpu-box # NVIDIA, or fail robin gui --encoder software build-box # never the GPU

By default the CLI picks the encoder from the probe. It takes the GPU when the host can drive it and the GPU pays for the latency it adds: on hosts with four cores or fewer, and for sessions above 1920x1080 when ffmpeg can drive the GPU. VA-API comes before NVENC. Everywhere else it stays in software. If the GPU it picked fails on the host, the session carries on in software, and `-v` shows which encoder was picked, why, and why it fell back. An encoder named with `--encoder` is used or the session fails.

The agent is a static binary and cannot load the host's GPU libraries, so for these it pipes frames through a tool the host already has: ffmpeg, or GStreamer's `gst-launch-1.0`. VA-API needs a render node in `/dev/dri` you can open (usually that means being in the `render` group) and either ffmpeg built with `h264_vaapi` or `gst-launch-1.0` with GStreamer's va or vaapi plugin and gst-plugins-good. NVENC needs the NVIDIA driver loaded, and ffmpeg with `h264_nvenc` or GStreamer's nvcodec plugin. On Debian and Ubuntu, `sudo apt install ffmpeg` brings both encoders. The CLI checks all of this against the probe before it deploys anything and says what is missing; the agent then tries each route the host offers on a test frame, ffmpeg first, and if none works the error lists why each one failed.
